Apezone · brand relaunch · Phase 2 · task 2.6

The brand
guide

Everything needed to make something that looks like Apezone: the mark and its files, the palette, the typeface, the layout grammar, how the photographs look, how the band writes, and what is off-limits. It is assembled from nine settled documents and adds no decisions of its own — including the ones it would rather not repeat.

This guide is an assembly of decisions already recorded elsewhere in brand/. It adds no new ones. The band has now seen the work (reported 2026‑08‑30) and responded to the direction — warmly to the illustrated material. That is not a signature on each rule here, and where a decision was taken inside a round it was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you have not seen it. The last section here lists what is not settled — six known defects, two open questions, and the four contradictions between source documents that assembling this turned up.

If you are making something

Read §0 and go straight to the section you need. Every number you are likely to want is on the card below; every file name is in §2. You should be able to lay out a gig poster correctly without opening anything else.

If you are in the band

This is the rulebook, not the pitch. The pitch is the overview, and it is the better read. What this page adds is the detail — and, at the end, an honest list of what is still broken or undecided.

Nine documents in brand/ hold the reasoning behind everything here: DIRECTION.md, BUILD-SPEC.md, platform.md, decisions.md, colour.md, typography.md, art-direction.md, logo-build/DECISIONS.md and assets/logos/USAGE.md. This page decides nothing they did not already decide.

§0

The card — everything in ten seconds

GroundInk #0A1116. This is a dark identity by default.
Text on InkBone only. Steel is 2.34:1 and fails. Hierarchy on dark comes from size, weight and position — there is no dimmer grey.

Glyph floor16 px, always on its Ink tile. Take the PNG cut for the size you are placing; never shrink a bigger one.
Clear spaceOne cap height all round the wordmark = 12.6% of its width. A quarter tile round the glyph, already built into the shipped tiles.
WarmthOne warm element per surface. A dash or a tick or a rule. Under 2% of the surface. Amber on dark only; Brass never on Bone.
TypeBarlow, weights 400 / 500 / 600 / 900. Nothing else.
NeverNo red · no stars near the skull · no skull inside the ring O · no crossbar on the chevron A · no bevel, glow, gradient, shadow or outline stroke · no stretching.

If the card and a section below ever disagree, the section is right and the card needs fixing.

The system — six elements, and they are not equals

Read this before the rest of the guide. The brand has six visual elements and a ranking, and using a good element in the wrong slot is the most likely way to get this wrong. The wordmark is the identity. Everything else supports it, decorates around it, or belongs to one campaign.

The two mistakes this table exists to prevent

1. The skull is not the primary symbol. It is the band's illustration. A reader who meets the skull first — on an avatar, on a plate, on a shirt — reasonably assumes it is the logo, and an outside review of these reports did exactly that in 2026-08-04. The word is the logo. The skull is what the word's band draws.

2. Six good ideas are not six identities. The rings, the pulse, the shards and the signs are all strong and all real, and none of them is the brand. They are ranked above for the same reason the palette allows one warm element per surface: a system where everything is a lead is a system with no lead. One large-format element per surface — rings or shards or a full-bleed photograph, never two.

This table decides nothing. Every row is DIRECTION.md's and names the conflict it was settled in, so it can be checked rather than trusted. It exists because the ranking was true in five places and stated in none.

§1

The band, in one paragraph

Apezone is a Helsinki five-piece that has been making heavy, groove-led rock since Easter 1997. Three of the five started it — in a café, drunk, on a whim — and are still in it. The fourth has been there fifteen years. In between there is a national tour, a decade off, an album that was finished and never released, and a concept EP about the man on the statue outside the National Theatre. That is not a career. It is a habit that never quite broke. In 2027 the band turns thirty and starts playing again.

The one-line version: Helsinki. Heavy. Since 1997. Still the same three men who started it.

The brand’s job is not to explain the gap, apologise for it, or dramatise the return. It is to make thirty years read as the advantage it plainly is. A band that announces it is dangerous is asking to be believed; a band that has been doing this since 1997, in the same rooms, with the same people, is not asking. Everything else in this guide — the restraint, the weight, the dryness — is downstream of that one fact.

Four things Apezone is never positioned as

A reunion. A nostalgia act. A joke band. A young band’s brand worn by men in their forties and fifties — that last one is the single most damaging thing this relaunch could do, and it is the specific failure the 2011–12 era fell into.

§2

The mark

APEZONE in letterspaced capitals: chevron A, plain ring O, stroke 24.0% of cap height. The band’s own 2013 letterforms at double the weight. Ratio 7.43:1 — it does not get stretched.

One system, five tiers. The lockup is the only tier without the skull; everything smaller carries it.

360 px — comfortable

Below 120 px seven letterspaced letters cannot survive. No craft fixes that — use the glyph instead.

Clear space

One cap height on all four sides. Cap is 148.70 units against a mark 1175.524 wide, so the working number is 12.6% of the placed width — 114 px round a 900 px lockup. The dashed line is the mark’s own box.

The date variant

The date is 1997–2027 — set in Barlow at ≈30% of cap height, centred, one cap height below the baseline. Lining figures, en dash U+2013, no spaces. Never a hyphen, never rebuilt in another face. Bone.

The 240 px floor is unenforceable on a baked image. A 1200×630 share card is shown at ~200 px in a chat preview and the whole surface scales with it, so the date becomes a smudge and the artefact cannot drop it. The floor holds for live surfaces that can respond; fixed-size share images carry the plain wordmark instead.

Two colourways, and above 48 px they are different geometry

The marks are strictly one colour: Bone on Ink (default) or Ink on Paper. There is no third state. But for the skull above 48 px, which shapes get the colour depends on the ground — the two are exact complements of one another inside the plate.

On Ink: the negative. The pale shapes give the mass and the eye sockets stay dark. Files: -bone and -white

On Paper and in print: the positive. The same drawing as dark linework; the paper gives the mass. Files: -ink and -black

Take the colourway that matches the background and the geometry comes with it. Crossing them — the negative on Paper, the positive on Ink — inverts the read and is wrong every time.

Do not change this

The chevron A is doing almost all of the work. The ownability test on 2026-08-02 set the same word in ordinary geometric sans faces, matched for cap, tracking and width. The mark is pickable out of that line-up instantly — and cover that one letter and the rest is close to Century Gothic Bold. The mark is distinctive in one letter and ordinary in six.

So: never reach for the crossbar. Any pressure to conventionalise that glyph — a legibility complaint, a well-meaning redraw — guts the mark rather than trimming it. The sanctioned fix for the Λ glance-pause is widening the chevron, and even that has a ceiling, because past a point widening also sands off the one distinguishing feature.

§3

The skull is two drawings, and that is a known defect

Below 48 px the identity switches to a different, simpler skull. Above 48 it is the f8 master — the front-only facial plate settled by rounds F and G. At 32, 24 and 16, and in all three frames of favicon.ico, it is round B’s r4b drawing instead.

They are close kin — both front-only, both crestless, one outline family — but they are not one object. Task 2.2b existed specifically to remove this, and it is back with the sizes swapped over. It is recorded as a knowing failure in logo-build/DECISIONS.md §8 rather than smoothed over.

Why, and it is the useful part

The big drawing was reduced down the ramp, shipped, and rejected on sight. Its eye sockets are gaps between strokes, not closed shapes, so they have no independent existence to preserve — reduce the linework and every feature disappears at once. r4b’s sockets are holes, and a hole survives reduction because it has its own edges.

Whether a drawing can be made small is decided when it is drawn, not when it is reduced.

What it means when you are placing one

  • Use the PNG cut for the size you are placing. Never shrink a big one. apezone-glyph-512.png scaled to 16 px is grey mush where apezone-glyph-16.png reads.
  • Do not put the 96 px badge and the 24 px one side by side and expect them to match. They will not, and that is a known cost rather than a bug to report.
  • At 16 px it reads as a skull, not specifically an ape skull. That was accepted deliberately — every 16 px artefact across three rounds de-specifies.
The split costs more than legibility — measured 2026-08-04

The point above — at 16 px it is a skull, not an ape skull — was always recorded as a legibility trade-off. It is also an ownability one, and that is the larger cost. Put the mark in a line-up of generic skull emblems and the big drawing is pickable instantly: it is the only one that is not a human skull, because every conventional skull emblem has a cranium and f8 has none. r4b at 96 px sits inside that family. At 32 px it is indistinguishable from it.

So the distinctiveness lives entirely in the large drawing. This is not a new defect — it sharpens the one this section already describes. And it is bounded: every social avatar is ≥320 px, so every avatar anyone sees is the drawing that passes. The conventional one appears at favicon and OS-icon sizes only. logo-build/DECISIONS.md §10.

Every tile at its own size, unmagnified. The drawing changes between 48 and 32.

§4

Colour

Two hues. A cold one at five values — 201°, the structure measured off the 2015 record — and one warm hue at two values. That is the whole system.

Ink#0A1116The ground. Default background everywhere.
Steel#3F5260Graphic mass and rules. Never text on Ink.
Bone#C6D2D6Primary text, and the reversed mark.
Slate#1B2830Raised surfaces and panels on Ink.
Paper#F2F1EELight-context ground — print, press kit.
Aged Brass#9C7C3CThe accent. The one warm hue.
Lamp Amber#D9B36AThe accent’s tint — dark grounds only.

The seven rules

  1. Ink is the default ground. This is a dark identity; the mark works better reversed than positive.
  2. The accent stays under 2% of any surface. More than a few percent and it has become the identity again.
  3. Steel is never text on Ink — 2.34:1. It is graphic mass: rules, large numerals, fields.
  4. The accent never touches the skull. Not as fill, not as outline, not as a disc behind it, and never with stars.
  5. No red anywhere, including “just a little” in photography grading or on merch. This governs the colour the brand chooses, not the colour the world is — so the RAG status set at the end of this section is scoped out of it, and so is a red cable in colour footage. On every graphic surface it is absolute.
  6. One accent per view. A hairline or a date or a marker — not all three at once.
  7. Amber on dark only. Brass off Bone.
The consequence of rule 3, and it constrains every dark surface

On Ink the palette has exactly one legal text colour, and it is Bone. Steel fails, Slate is a ground, and both warm tokens live under a 2% ceiling. So hierarchy on dark comes from size, weight, tracking and position — never from a dimmer grey, because there isn’t one. C5’s own poster broke this three times and the rebuild had to fix it.

WCAG 2.1 relative-luminance maths, computed rather than estimated. AA = 4.5:1 body, 3:1 large; AAA = 7:1.

Before anything is printed

Aged Brass is unproofed in CMYK and will disappoint. Gold-family colours go flat, dull and slightly green in four-colour process. For merch, patches, or anything where the accent carries weight, specify a spot colour and get a physical proof. Do not order printed merch on the strength of a screen render, or a soft proof.

Three more print facts. Ink is a rich black at 169% total coverage and will not match a printer’s default K — send -K100.pdf for one-colour work. Bone reads as plain grey on coated stock; on uncoated, consider letting the paper be Bone and not printing it at all. And Ink against Slate is 1.26:1 — nearly identical on cheap panels, in sunlight, and after social recompression, so never use that step alone to communicate structure. Add a Steel hairline.

The CMYK values in colour.md are unmanaged arithmetic with no profile and no rendering intent. No Pantone references have been invented.

Status colours — RAG, and they are not the palette

A page that reports state needs red-amber-green, because it is a convention the reader already knows: a status chip should mean the same thing here as anywhere else. So these three sit deliberately outside the two hues, and they are the one place this brand uses a green.

What rule 5 does and does not reach. “No red anywhere” governs the colour the brand chooses for its own surfaces — artwork, type, rules, fields, merch, grading. It does not reach a FAIL cell in a measurement table or a status badge on the site, because a measurement outcome is not the brand talking. Full scope in colour.md §8.

The same scope covers colour footage — settled 2026-08-04. A teaser is a record of a room, and the room was not specified by anybody, so a red amp jewel or a red cable is not a rule-5 breach. What stays forbidden is red the production chooses: red dressed into a shot, grading toward red, or a red field. And rule 5 is absolute again on every graphic laid over the footage — end card, type, rules, scrims. The footage is a record; the graphics on it are the brand. art-direction.md §9.4.

Pass#2F6B4F / #6FAF8Clight / dark — 5.57:1 · 7.41:1
Warn#6B6318 / #CFB84Elight / dark — 5.43:1 · 9.61:1
Fail#8A3B2A / #D08C77light / dark — 6.79:1 · 6.97:1
Three rules, and the first one is the trap

1. On a Slate panel, use the dark value whatever the page theme is. The light values fail on Slate — pass 2.40:1, fail 1.97:1 — and Slate’s whole job is raised surfaces and panels. This has never bitten because the reports only put light-mode text on Paper, and it will bite the first status badge on a Slate card.

2. Colour is never the only signal. Every use in these reports sits on a word that already says it — FAIL, Pending, no, Ships. Warn and the accent are separated by hue and share the same lightness on purpose, so a bare coloured dot with no label is not readable for everyone. Label it, or give it a shape.

3. Aged Brass and Lamp Amber are never a status. They are the identity’s warm hue. If a status needs warmth it uses Warn. Until 2026-08-03 dark-mode warn was Lamp Amber — the same colour as the accent, ΔE 0.00 — so the brand’s one point of warmth and “needs attention” were indistinguishable. Warn moved to ~50° at matched lightness, so nothing on any page changed weight.

§5

Type

One family: Barlow (Jeremy Tribby, SIL OFL 1.1). Black 900 display, Regular 400 text, Medium 500 and SemiBold 600 supporting. No second family, and no other weights — the subsets carry exactly these four, so adding one means re-subsetting.

It wins on a measurement: Barlow Black’s stem is 26.9% of cap height against the mark’s 24.0% — inside the mark’s own acceptance band. Heavier faces out-muscle the mark; lighter ones are the thin geometric the whole redraw was correcting.

Everything below is set in the real shipping WOFF2 files, embedded in this page.

The rules that matter most

  1. The display face never sets the word APEZONE. The wordmark is bespoke outlines from the band’s own letterforms. Barlow sits beside it, never replaces it. This is a gate, not a preference — it is what gate 5 caught C5’s poster doing.
  2. Reversed text floor: Regular holds at ≥14 px on Ink. Below that, Medium. Barlow Regular is a light text face — stem 10.1% of cap — and this rule exists because of that measurement.
  3. Tabular, lining figures everywhere numbers stack: gig listings, discography, the record line, the pulse caption. The CSS is font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums lining-nums
  4. Letterspacing: caps labels +0.14–0.18em; display caps near-normal; lowercase never letterspaced. The wide-tracked voice belongs to the mark and the record line only — headings do not imitate it.
  5. Case: display and labels may be caps; headings default to sentence case. No exclamation marks rescued by big type.
  6. Self-hosted always. The site loads the WOFF2 subsets from brand/fonts/woff2/ — no CDN, no Google Fonts runtime request.
In running text the band is Apezone, not APEZONE

Full capitals in a sentence is the tell of a band trying to be loud on the page. The capital form appears only as the mark itself — and in the record line, which is furniture rather than prose.

§6

Layout — the C5 grammar

The application grammar is adopted whole, and it is mark-independent: it takes the wordmark, the glyph or a release sign equally. Four pieces of furniture, and four rules about how they sit together.

ElementWhat it is
Record line APEZONE · HELSINKI · 1997–2027, letterspaced caps, one line, at the top or bottom of a surface like a colophon. The en dash is the warm element — Amber on dark, Brass on paper.
Pulse rule The 31-station documented-activity strip. The 2027 tick is always hollow and is always the surface’s one amber element when present. Its one-sentence caption appears once per medium, findably. The data changes only if band-facts.md changes.
Stamp Bordered plate: APEZONE / EST. EASTER 1997 · HELSINKI. Legible at ≥96 px; does not exist below.
Date furniture Venues and dates set huge and tabular, signage register — and the band’s real places and dates only. Finnish for home-audience surfaces.

The four rules

  1. One warm element per surface. A dash or a tick or a rule — never two. Absolute.
  2. Precedence: when the pulse rule is present, its hollow amber tick is the surface’s one warm element and the record-line dash sets in Bone. This rule exists because C5’s own poster carried both, measured.
  3. The lockup answers the pulse rule’s measure. Where the two share a surface, the lockup is ≥60% of the pulse rule’s width. At C5’s own 29% share the mark reads as a caption to its own furniture. On A3 the number that works is 900 px against a 1470 px measure — 61%.
  4. The record line does not sit adjacent to the lockup. Its first word is the band’s name, so beside the mark the surface says it twice about 100 px apart, and the line reads as a caption repeating the thing above it. Opposite ends of a surface — masthead and imprint — is fine, and is how it is specified.
One more thing gate 5 established

On a 1200×630 header the 120 px floor never binds. The binding constraint is a ceiling of 958 px, set by clear space at the sides — an eight-to-one range to compose in. With the date variant the ceiling drops to 851 px.

Two large-format elements — and both are surfaces, not marks

Neither is in assets/logos/, because neither is a mark. Both are inputs to the website (Phase 4) and merch (3.6).

For merch they are not interchangeable, and the reason is a licence. The shard fields are generated images, and the merchandise licence covering them excludes AI-generated resources — absent it, an AI resource on merchandise has to be a secondary element rather than the main visual focus. On a shirt back the artwork is the main visual focus. The rings are zero generations. So only the rings can be the main event on a garment; a shard field there is a background behind something else, or it is not used.

The rings — large-format only, and not as a preference

Website hero, anniversary poster, vinyl label, stage backdrop, shirt back. It is the most beautiful object round C produced, and it is beautiful because it is true.

It dies as a mark. A visible moiré rosette already at 96 px, a circle with a dot; nothing left at 48 or 16. And simplifying it for small sizes defeats the data, so the answer is never to use it small rather than to draw a small version.

The floor is measured, in millimetres and in pixels. The thinnest ink in the drawing is a silent year at 0.131% of the artwork’s width — twenty-one of the thirty-one years are silent, so the floor is set by the years when nothing happened. That is 0.366 mm on a 280 mm shirt back. Never below 250 mm on fabric, or 800 px on screen. Whether 0.4 mm survives your process is a question for the printer, not for this guide.

One colour is a real colourway — rings-mono-ink.svg is the screen-print master, and the 2027 ring is drawn as a genuine void so that it still means not yet once the amber is gone.

It needs its one sentence, once, findably: one ring per year since Easter 1997. Without it the encoding is invisible. Same treatment as the pulse caption and the Kivi sentence; final wording in task 4.3.

Count the rings and the biography audits — so the data changes only if band-facts.md changes, and rings-build/check_activity.py now fails the build if it has. assets/large-format/rings/ — six colourways, SVG masters. 2026 is drawn silent: the reassembly to five is not a gig, a release or a recorded work.

The shards — in, and this is where they go

Shard fields are a sanctioned element, not a rejected one. They work as a background, with the mark or the type in the calm centre — and not always with the skull. Website hero is the case they were validated for; large-format print and merch are the same register. Nothing here rules them out on the web or on a release.

What follows are three rules about how, not whether. All three come from what went wrong the first time round, and none of them is a matter of taste.

  1. A real Ink scrim goes behind any type on a shard field — roughly 75% Ink over the type’s own footprint, feathered out. No exceptions. The rule exists because a mock once claimed a scrim it had never built: the legibility was coming from the artwork’s own dark centre, and the subline was already marginal where shards cut behind it. Demonstrated and measured 2026-08-03 by task 3.7, which also had to reword it — the old version said 75% at centre, radial, and that fails: four fifths of the way down a hero the radial has decayed to 43% Ink, and 3 of 456 test placements on the then-cold fields came out at 3.47:1, below AA for small text. Keep a radial wash as well — it is what makes the centre calm. On the gold fields that shipped, this rule is load-bearing rather than prudent: Bone on Lamp Amber is 1.28:1, a bare gold field measures 1.00:1 under every line of type on it, and every one of 100 placements fails without the wash. With it, 0 of 100 fail and the worst is 8.43:1.
  2. Production shard fields are re-made deliberately — own artwork, palette-exact, compressed. The round-C files are concept images and those particular files do not ship as final artwork; the idea does, rebuilt. Built 2026-08-03, and they are gold — take a field from assets/large-format/shards/. There is one per shape of surface, and they run edge to edge with no calm centre baked in — the scrim makes the calm middle where type needs it, so the artwork is usable bare as well. Never crop one field into another ratio: the fracture and the calm centre are both built for the ratio they were made at, so re-render for a new size and generate a new source for a new shape. The fields are generated images snapped onto the five palette values — five colours, zero stray pixels, and 0.000% red against 0.39–2.27% in the raw generations, because a generated gold reliably drifts orange. A gold field that has not been through that snap is not a brand asset.
  3. Stars come out. The linocut and hybrid pieces carry skull + stars — two thirds of the 2011 badge, which the identity decisions forbid from reassembling. Any production version strips them.
  4. The field is the surface's one warm element. A shard field is far past §3's 2% accent ceiling by design and by Marcus's decision of 2026-08-03, so nothing else on that surface may be warm: the record-line dash sets in Bone. Identical precedence to the pulse rule. And put a real Ink wash behind any type — rule 1 above, which matters far more here than it ever did on a cold field, because Bone on Lamp Amber is 1.28:1 and a bare gold field measures 1.00:1 under every line of type on it.

Rule 2 is about the files, not the idea. Re-making a field deliberately is how the idea gets used properly — not a reason to leave it alone.

A shard sleeve is an extension, and it needs Marcus’s call

Website hero and large-format print are covered. Release artwork is not, quite. Since the 2026-08-30 restructure a shard field is listed as an element rather than a missing composition — so the question is no longer whether to invent a fourth sleeve, but which route it sits inside. It is not forbidden; it has simply never been approved for a sleeve, so this guide cannot present it as settled.

The obvious way to do it is the photograph route’s structure with a shard field where the photograph goes: field, a real Ink scrim into the bottom ~42%, mark at ~46% of the sleeve width, record line at the top carrying the warm dash. That reuses a layout that already works and breaks no rule above — but what a record may look like is a call about the records, so it is Marcus’s, not the guide’s. And the licence limit holds either way: the fields are generated, so one may not be the main visual focus of merchandise.

And the loud register does have a home

Quiet mark, loud frame. A dense screen-print poster or a tour shirt in the maximalist register — shards, linocut, carved rays — sitting inside an otherwise restrained system reads as a band having fun with its own iconography. Tested honestly against the restrained work, and the restrained work read more confident beside it, not less.

The failure mode was never loud artefacts. It was a loud identity. So: one-off merch and posters, governed by the system. Never the identity, and never the mark.

§7

Photography

Shoot the band the way you would shoot five men who have been doing this for thirty years and are not trying to impress you. Available light, wide enough to see the room, nobody lit. Ask the venue for white front light, because a coloured stage wash cannot be graded and the frame is lost at the moment of capture. Include hands, cases, cables and empty rooms, not only faces. The finished pictures are black and white with a cold cast in the shadows, and they go all the way from true black to true white — on a dark page the photograph is the thing that carries the light. If you grade your own work to that, nothing here touches it.

The narrow version of the rule, which is more useful than “shoot documentary”: arrange the people. Do not light them, and do not fix them afterwards. Posing is fine — the best frame in the whole archive is posed. Lighting and retouching are what is off-limits.

The one instruction that has to be given before the shoot

Ask the venue for white or near-white front light, at least for the first three songs — or shoot in a room the band controls. Say it when the gig is booked, not on the night. A frame under saturated coloured wash does not become restrained in monochrome, it becomes fog, and no amount of processing recovers it. Global contrast does not catch this; mid-tone texture does. grade.gradeability() scores usable frames 0.093–0.130 and washed ones 0.019–0.061, with the threshold at 0.070. Run it over a take before anyone starts selecting.

Consequence worth knowing before a campaign is planned around archive imagery: much of the existing live archive is coloured wash and cannot be brought to brand quality.

PropertySpecification
ColourMonochrome. A cold cast in the shadows only, falling off so black is palette-cold and white stays white. A cast carried into the highlights is a duotone, and a duotone makes every frame look like the same picture.
RangeTrue black to true white. Black point 0.02, white 0.98. No clamp at either end.
ContrastPreserved, with a quarter-strength S. Not compressed.
Blue28% of the luma weight moved to the blue channel, so a blue-lit room keeps its structure instead of going to mud. Every Finnish club is a blue-lit room at some point in the evening.
Grain0.030, applied last, at final output size. Present when you look for it, absent when you don’t. At 0.050 it announces itself; at 0.080 it is an effect. Grain is the only texture allowed inside a photograph.
PresenceAt least 3.0:1 against the Ink page. Some frames cannot clear it because they are genuinely dark rooms — the answer there is composition, not more processing. Do not run them full-bleed.
A photographer who already grades well is left alone

This is a specification a photographer works to, first, and a piece of software second. Hand them the numbers above; they will do it better than a script because they were in the room. conforms() checks a delivered frame and usually returns leave it alone. grade() is for material with nothing behind it: phone frames, archive scans, whatever the band shoots itself.

This is not a style note. The first version of this task ran its own treatment over an already-graded 2012 set and flattened it — the photographer’s untouched file beat the processed one. Re-processing finished work is on the off-limits list.

Release artwork

Three compositions, all 1:1, all Ink ground, all inside the grammar in §6 rather than beside it.

  • A — photograph, full bleed. Graded frame, a real Ink scrim into the bottom ~42%, mark at ~46% of the sleeve width, record line at the top carrying the warm dash. Use when the record has a documentary subject.
  • B — pictogram. One release sign, title in Barlow Black beneath, record line with a Bone dash because the sign already holds the surface’s amber. Use when the record has a joke or an idea. Provisionally adopted — see §10.
  • C — type only. No image. Title at ~12.8% of the sleeve, one small warm line beneath. Use when there is nothing honest to photograph. For a fourteen-year-old shelved album, that is the truthful answer.

Video and teasers

Added 2026-08-03, task 5.5. Full reasoning in art-direction.md §9; everything here is untested, because no Apezone footage exists to test it on. The first rehearsal is the first chance to falsify it.

  • In colour — Marcus’s call, 2026-08-03. The photographs stay black and white; the videos do not follow them.
  • Not graded. There is no specification for what a colour Apezone picture looks like, so grading toward one would be inventing it. But “leave it as is” is a trap: a phone gives you its grade — saturation lifted, contrast pushed, sharpening, drifting auto white balance — and §9 already forbids the look of a phone’s auto-enhance. So the work moves to capture: lock the white balance (neutral, not “as shot”), turn the enhancement off, lock exposure. Afterwards, fix white balance if it drifted and nothing else.
  • No LUT, no filter, no cinematic preset. §9’s ban on theatrical grading covers all of it.
  • No grain — grain goes on last at final output size, and on video the platform re-encodes after you, so grain buys a worse picture and a bigger file.
  • Red is the rule colour puts under strain, and the scope is now settled. Monochrome satisfied no red anywhere by construction; a camera in a real room does not. Adopted 2026-08-04: rule 5 governs the colour the brand chooses — no red dressed in, no grading toward red, no red field — and stays absolute on every graphic laid over the footage. A red cable is the room and is fine. The footage is a record; the graphics on it are the brand.
  • Still turn the coloured bulb off. A red-washed frame was ungradeable in black and white; in colour it is simply red all over, which is worse.
  • No permanent corner bug. That is broadcast behaviour. An end card only when the clip has something to announce — Ink, the mark, the pulse rule, 1.5–2 seconds, and nothing on it that has to be read.
  • Shoot once, vertically, composed to the centre square, so a 1:1, 4:5 or 16:9 crop all survive. Never shoot a camera mono profile — mono capture is destructive and a rehearsal cannot be restaged.
  • Type: Bone only, over a real scrim, and the clip must work with it unread. Use the platform’s own captions rather than burning them in.
  • The audio is the subject. A teaser with bad sound fails whatever it looks like. A phone microphone in a loud room clips, and that cannot be repaired afterwards.
§7b

Illustrated artwork — covers and posters

This is the default for covers and posters, and you may reach for it. Adopted 2026-08-30. A cover or a poster is its own artwork, made for that song or that story — a generated illustration in a limited-ink screenprint register, finished by a fixed set of treatments. The band saw this direction and it is the part they responded to most.

It has its own colours, and that is the point. colour.md decision 18 suspends the palette rules inside the picture on these surfaces: no 2% accent ceiling, no forbidden hue. A cover may be hot pink. What it may not do is bring those colours back out onto a website, a profile or a document — those stay on the palette, and a platform carries one picture’s world at a time, never a mixture.

Brief it as a situation, not a portrait — this is where the humour lives

The band’s humour lives in the releases, not in the mark, and this is the thing that carries it. A piece is briefed as something happening: driving a stolen catering cart through the barrier, making off with an entire sausage grill, a burnout through the middle of the bike camp, cutting a mooring rope with an axe. The joke is in the situation; the drawing stays dead straight. Böbbis never mugs, never poses, never looks at the viewer — which is exactly why this does not collide with §9. A gag announces itself; a situation does not.

A portrait is the failure mode, and that is measured rather than asserted: when Böbbis was the subject rather than one actor in an event, half the frames put his head where the wordmark goes, and the pictures were weaker. And this is the one step nothing here can do for you — every other layer has machinery behind it. The generator will return a competent scene forever; it will never return the idea.

What goes on top of every generation

The mechanism is constant; the result is different every time, because each treatment is measured from the picture it is applied to.

  • The real wordmark. The shipped master supplies the letterforms — always. Its colour and its surface treatment are both decided for that poster by a person. A measurement can refuse either; it never makes the choice. Picking the best-scoring treatment instead returned the same one on six pictures out of six. Compose the treatment for the picture from the kit of parts — an outline, a stroke, a stripe, an offset ghost, a gradient, a glow. The eight built-in treatments are worked examples to read, not a list to pick from: a menu is what made every poster look alike. Blue is not a default, and neither is cream.
  • One legibility rule, and it says nothing about light or dark. The mark must separate from the artwork underneath it — by its letterforms or by its outline, whichever is doing the work — checked in six bands down the letterform so a treatment cannot die at one end and be rescued by its average. So a dark wordmark on a dark picture is fine if it carries a light stroke. The one thing that genuinely fails is a flat mark, no outline, whose brightness matches its background.
  • A halftone screen, where the source needs one. The share is an output of what the mask selects, not a number anyone sets.
  • Böbbis, in one of his two forms.

One thing belongs to the generation and never to the treatment: the medium. Dots added afterwards are a treatment inside artwork already drawn in the right register — they are never a way to convert rendered digital art into a screenprint. If a source comes back glossy, with smooth gradients and volumetric light, regenerate it. Do not texture the mistake away.

Do not move more of the finishing into the generation, however capable the model looks. Medium belongs in the drawing — ink, grain, halftone — because applied afterwards it reads as a filter. Everything else belongs after it, for a blunt reason: the model has no seed, so a generation can never be made again, while everything applied afterwards can be re-run forever. Move work into the generation and you are trading artwork you can reproduce for artwork you cannot.

Böbbis is two devices, and both are in use

  • The emblem — the skull alone, placed in the scene on a real surface: steam, a flight-case badge, a television, a cassette label. Small, never the subject, never where the wordmark goes.
  • The character — Böbbis with a body: skeleton, worn clothes, the guitar across his back so both hands are free. An actor inside the event. This is the default.

Which one is a judgement about the picture, not a quota. The character leads; the emblem is for a composition that wants a mark rather than a figure — a hero object dead centre, a surface asking for a badge, a frame with nowhere for someone to stand. And where neither fits, use neither: a forced placement is worse than none.

Watch one thing. The emblem is the easier device, so “it fits the composition better” can quietly become “it was less work.” Say which device a picture uses and why.

Every generation with the character uses the approved drawing as an image reference, not a description. Words alone grow a cranium, a human chin and hair — that is measured, not a hunch. He is dead serious, never mugs, never poses. Nothing crosses his mouth.

And what this does not license

  • The illustrated skull is not the logo. It never appears where the glyph goes and never replaces it. Social avatars, favicons and the website keep the shipped glyph — it is the one that was engineered to survive 16 px, and that is an accessibility decision rather than a stylistic one.
  • Nothing here may be printed or sold. Decision 12 still blocks it, and the shops are a separate question again. Screen only.
  • The straight-face rule survives intact. A cartoonish register is not permission for a gag — see §9. It has been tested four times and held four times.
  • He is never named in public. Settled 2026-08-30 and it now covers the character, not just the glyph: in files he is Böbbis, in public he is the ape skull or nothing. A named mascot announces the joke.
  • The band endorsed a direction, not each picture. Individual covers and posters are still approved one at a time.
§8

Voice

The identity stays straight. The humour lives in the writing, the releases and the videos — that is a settled division, not an oversight. A mark that tries to be funny does the joke for you, lands once, and makes every serious thing afterwards look like a setup.

Where that meets §9’s ban on visual gags, which it looks like it contradicts, the line is: the camera never tells the joke, but the band can. Every item on the banned list — a banana, a gorilla suit, ape hands, a wink — is a prop or a gesture somebody has to bring. The rule governs what the production does. It has never governed what happens in the room, and it cannot, because §9’s own closing test is would a joke survive being placed in this frame? So the frame stays straight, the room is allowed to be funny, and the edit reveals rather than manufactures — no zoom-in, freeze-frame, record scratch or on-screen arrow, because those are the camera doing it. One absolute: the ape is never the joke.

The six rules

  1. State the fact and stop. The facts here are unusually good — twenty-three gigs in 2000, a garden in 2011, nine songs nobody has heard. Adjectives make them smaller.
  2. Let the reader do the arithmetic. Write 1997–2027, not “an incredible thirty years”.
  3. The joke goes at the end, and it is not flagged. No exclamation marks, no emoji, no “haha”. A dry line landing after a plain one is the whole technique.
  4. First person, plural, unglamorous. We played, we recorded, we didn’t release it. Third-person band-bio voice is for other people to write — the press kit is the one exception.
  5. Never assert heaviness. No “bone-crushing”, “relentless”, “brutal”. If the music is heavy the reader will find out; if the copy says so, the reader assumes it isn’t.
  6. Write English that a Finn would actually write. Clear, short, slightly clipped, no American rock-press idiom. Occasional slightly-off phrasing is character, not error.
Words we use

Played. Recorded. Started again. Shelved. Finished. Never released. Same room. The archive. Thirty years. Helsinki.

Words we don’t

Reunion. Comeback. Legendary. Iconic. Journey. Finally. Long-awaited. Back with a vengeance. Bigger and better. Sorry for the silence.

The examples below are voice patterns, not approved copy

Dates and details in them are placeholders. Nothing here goes out without the underlying fact being checked — and several facts in the band’s own history are still contested. No former member is named in public copy without their agreement.

Gig announcement — English

Karkkila, Rautaruukki. [date].
We played this room in 1999, in 2000, and again in 2011. Doors 20:00.
Same band, mostly.

Gig announcement — Finnish, written rather than translated

Karkkila, Rautaruukki. [pvm].
Soitettiin tässä salissa 1999, 2000 ja 2011. Ovet 20:00.
Sama bändi, enimmäkseen.

Sama bändi, enimmäkseen is a Finnish joke, not an English one carried across. That is the whole of the language policy in one line.

The shelved album, if it goes out

Tomorrow Is A New Day.
Recorded in 2013. Mixed, sleeved, and prepared for pressing. Then not released.
Thirteen songs. Four of them came out in other forms. The other nine have never left the band.
They will on [date].

NeverWhyInstead
“We’re BACK and heavier than ever!!!”Announces force instead of having it.“Karkkila, Rautaruukki. [date].”
“After 30 incredible years…”Tells the reader how to feel about a number they can read.“1997–2027.”
“Bone-crushing riffs and relentless aggression.”Press-release English.Say what was recorded, where, and when.
“Monkey business as usual”Comedy-monkey. The name walks straight into it.Cut the animal joke entirely.
“Sorry we’ve been quiet!”Apologises for the most interesting part of the story.State the years flatly, or say nothing.
Machine-translated FinnishReads as careless in a country where everyone will notice.Write it in Finnish, or don’t.
Language, in one table’s worth of words

English primary, Finnish as support — not a mirrored bilingual site. English for the website, release titles, streaming metadata and the international press kit. Finnish for gig announcements at home, archive posts, and the Finnish press kit. Never machine-translate. Place names stay Finnish; names keep their diacritics everywhere, including in English copy.

§9

Off limits

The section to read before starting anything. Nothing here is a stylistic preference; each item is in the list because it is somewhere in the band’s own archive and it is what the relaunch is defined against.

On the mark

  • No crossbar on the A.
  • No skull inside the O.
  • No stars within sight of the skull — two thirds of the 2011 badge, and it does not get reassembled by accident.
  • No effects: no bevel, glow, gradient, drop shadow or outline stroke. (An outline on a mid-tone or busy ground is a separate per-surface layer, not part of the mark.)
  • No recolouring beyond the four supplied files. Never Steel for the mark.
  • No stretching. The wordmark is 7.43:1 and stays there.
  • The skull is never red, and it is never publicly named — and since 2026-08-30 that covers the illustrated character too, not only the glyph. In files he is Böbbis; in public he is the ape skull, or nothing.

In the picture

  • Red. Anywhere. Including as a shadow tint, a “warm grade”, or one red object allowed to stay red. In a photograph — the stills are monochrome, so the object cannot survive the conversion anyway. Colour footage is scoped (2026-08-04): a red cable in a rehearsal room is the room, and what is forbidden there is red the production chooses. Graphics over the footage are absolute. art-direction.md §9.4.
  • Theatrical grading — crushed blacks, blown highlights, heavy grain, smoke as a subject.
  • Glossy retouching — sharpening, saturation pushes, skin smoothing, sky replacement, a phone’s auto-enhance. Thirty years is the asset.
  • Re-processing work that is already finished.
  • Clamping a photograph’s highlights to protect nearby type. Use a scrim behind the type instead.
  • Added texture of any kind — paper overlays, dust and scratches, light leaks, halation, torn edges, vignettes, lens flare.
  • Menace announced rather than implied — blood, barbed wire, fog machines, chains, snarling.
  • Visual gags. No monkey comedy, no banana, no gorilla suit, nothing that winks. This is the rule most likely to be argued with and it should not be.
  • Anything that reads as adolescent.

In the caption and the credit

  • Invented captions. No Latin binomials, no plate numbers, no institution names, no fabricated archive references, no invented dates. This applies to photograph credits exactly as much as to specimen plates.
  • Unverified identification. Do not caption a photograph with who is in it unless someone who was there has confirmed it.
  • Naming former members without their agreement.

In production

  • Generated photographs of the band. Four real, identifiable people. That job needs a camera.
  • Generated imagery presented as archival. Anything generated is labelled generated, every time, in the file name and in the caption.
  • Stock photography of people. A stock band is worse than no photograph.
  • No tagline. Monkey Business since 1997 and Music From / For Raging Apes are archive quotations only. Neither goes in a lockup, a header, a bio or a shirt.
The test that catches what a list cannot

Would a joke survive being placed in this frame?

If a dry caption or a daft release sleeve would look like a mistake against the imagery, the art direction has gone too solemn. The imagery’s job is to be a straight enough frame that the jokes land — not to be so funereal that they read as errors.

§10

Credits and licences

The ape skull

Drawn by Juha Syrjänen, of Honey Hellraiser. He drew it as a favour, for the B.A.M.F. EP, in early 2012 — not commissioned, not paid, and not licensed in any way. He is happy for the band to do as they wish with it and wants no say in what it became.

He should be named wherever the mark’s history is told. He did not ask to be; that is not a reason to leave him out. His original file no longer exists, so the band’s archive is everything that survives of it.

Nothing was written down at the time, which is normal for a favour between musicians. The one moment it could matter is a trademark registration, or a label or distributor asking the band to warrant that it owns the mark — both would want this on paper rather than remembered.

Barlow

SIL Open Font License 1.1. © 2017 The Barlow Project Authors, by Jeremy Tribby. No Reserved Font Name is declared, so the subsets do not need renaming, and the OFL permits embedding and conversion to outlines.

Two obligations travel with that: the fonts are never sold on their own, and OFL.txt travels with any redistribution of the files. It is in brand/fonts/.

The date in the lockup is Barlow Medium converted to outlines. No live type ships in any master.

What is bespoke, and what is not

  • P E Z N E — mechanical. The band’s own 2013 outlines, offset. Every curve is theirs, moved.
  • The A — reconstructed from the 2013 letter’s own measured skeleton, with two numbers changed.
  • The O — constructed. New geometry; the 2013 file has the skull in that slot.
  • The skull — weaker provenance than the wordmark, and it should be stated that way. The silhouette was re-plotted from a generated raster, de-barbed and symmetrised; the sockets are Juha’s curves; the nasal is authored. The small drawing is a traced generated glyph from round B. An originality check on the skull is still outstanding.
§11

What this guide does not settle

A guide that hides its defects is worse than one that explains them. Three groups: what is knowingly broken or unchecked, what is open and not this document’s to decide, and the four places where the source documents contradicted each other — found while assembling this, and since fixed.

Known defects, knowingly shipped

The skull is two drawings Split at 48 px. §3. The gate that existed to prevent this fails, and Marcus took two kin drawings over one unreadable ramp.
Aged Brass is unproofed in CMYK It appears in none of the logo files, but it will reach merch through the system furniture. Spot colour and a physical proof before anything is ordered.
Nothing has been seen in print Not on paper, not at physical size, not on a real phone. Every size claim in this guide is an exact-pixel render. Print one sheet before signing anything off.
The favicon has never been seen in a real tab The last thing owed on the glyph, and it is one command — serve assets/logos/favicon/tab-test/ and judge the 16 px icon in the tab strip, not on the page. Blob, goggles or gas mask is a fail. The fallback if it fails is the bare chevron.
The Ink scrim — demonstrated, and the rule reworded Closed 2026-08-03 by task 3.7, and it did not pass first time. The rule as written — 75% at centre, radial — failed at 3.47:1, because it fixes the value at one point and says nothing about the falloff. The scrim is now specified by the type rather than by the surface: 75% over the glyphs’ own footprint. Measured on the four shipped gold fields at 25 heights each: 0 of 100 fail, worst 8.43:1, against 100 of 100 and a worst of 1.00:1 bare. §6 rule 1, and brand/large-format/verify_scrim.py.
The large-format skull — asked for a third colour, and refused Opened and closed 2026-08-03. Task 3.2 built three continuous-tone materials for the big skull and every one needs Steel plus a mid-grey, because a lit surface cannot be described in two values — so each of them breaks §3's two states and no third. Marcus saw the comparison and declined the exception: “No I don’t like the other ones. The engraving is good for now.” The shipped plate is engraved, which takes its material from hatching and is therefore still exactly Ink on Paper — measured, zero Steel pixels. Worth knowing before anyone proposes it again: it has been asked, with artwork. brand/large-format/FINDINGS.md §1.4.
⚠ Generated artwork now ships, and the merchandise licence excludes it Opened 2026-08-03 and this one blocks merch. The shard fields are generated images. Their generator's own terms say that on merchandise sold to multiple buyers the content “must be a secondary element of the design — not the main visual focus”, and that the Merchandise Licence which lifts that restriction “covers non-AI Premium files only. AI-generated resources are excluded.” Website, social and unsold posters are fine. A shard field as the whole graphic on a shirt appears not to be covered, and a trademark application is not addressed at all. Three routes in brand/large-format/FINDINGS.md §4.2 — get it in writing, make the field secondary, or use one of the two non-generated fields in large-format/retired/. Needs a qualified opinion, not a designer's guess.
The circular avatar mask cut the small skull — fixed 2026-08-10 Found 2026-08-03 by task 3.3 and measured: the glyph tiles were inset to 86% of the tile, which is composed for a square, and an inscribed circle misses the corners — where round B’s brow tips sit. apezone-glyph-circle-16, -24 and -32 lost 1.7–2.1% of their ink. Two things were wrong with the diagnosis, and both mattered. The proposed remedy, inset 0.817, was solved at 512 px and would not have fixed the small files — at that inset the 24 px tile still clips 1.77% and the 32 px 1.05%, because each tile is rasterised at its own size. And clipping was never the whole failure: the detailed skull lost 0.00% yet cleared the mask by only 0.23% of the radius, and an antialiased edge meeting a hard boundary reads as an edge that was cut — which is how Marcus spotted it, on an avatar. The circle tiles now carry their own inset (0.82 detailed, 0.78 small) and a 3% optical drop, because 65% of this drawing’s ink sits above its own centre line. Nothing clips, and the closest any tile comes to the mask is 8.8%. Squares, favicon frames, transparent glyphs, headers and print files are untouched.
Every rule about video is untested §7 now covers teasers, and no Apezone footage exists — the archive holds 254 photographs and not one video file. Nothing has been tried on a phone either: which enhancement settings can be turned off, and whether white balance can be locked at all, is camera-specific and unchecked. The first rehearsal is the first chance to prove any of it wrong, and it is written so that it can be.
Colour video and the no-red rule — scoped, and settled “No red anywhere” was free while video was black and white, and stopped being free when the teasers went to colour, because a camera in a real rehearsal room records red objects. Settled 2026-08-04: rule 5 governs the colour the brand chooses, not the colour the world is — no red dressed into a shot, no grading toward red, no red field — and it is absolute again on every graphic laid over the footage. The footage is a record; the graphics on it are the brand. colour.md rule 5 and art-direction.md §9.4.
The record line’s string is fixed Where a surface genuinely needs the line and the lockup adjacent, dropping the name (HELSINKI · 1997–2027) is the fix — but that is off-spec and needs Marcus’s call.

Open, and not this guide’s to decide

  1. The pictogram programme is retired — settled 2026-08-30, and this is no longer open. It was provisionally adopted on 2026-08-03 pending Manu, Jukka and Tuomas, because the 1999 hazard-sign joke predates Marcus. The whole material went to the band in July 2026, and the answer came back: “C1 was not interesting to anyone.” So there is no per-release sign, and no content commitment that every record carry a one-line idea drawable as a road sign. What survives is the vocabulary, not the system — a warning sign may appear inside a generated picture as scene content, the way the skull appears as a badge on a flight case. Never a composited layer, never a device a release owes.
    The gap it leaves is real and unassigned: C1 was the only structural home three design rounds built for the humour, and nothing has replaced it.
  2. Which Nummela 2012 frames are Apezone. 197 full-resolution frames, white key light, gradeable — the best live material the band has. But Apezone played that night as the warm-up for Honey Hellraiser, so the shoot covers two bands and a whole evening, and the folder does not distinguish them. Nothing from it can be published as a picture of Apezone until someone who was there says which frames are which. This needs Marcus or another member, and it blocks the best photography in the archive.

Where the sources contradicted each other

Four found while assembling this, and all four are now fixed at source — on 2026-08-03, after Marcus read them. Every one turned out to be stale text rather than a live dispute: a sentence that was true when it was written and was overtaken by later work. They are listed here rather than deleted because how each one survived is the useful part, and because a reader holding an older copy of a source document needs to know which sentence to distrust.

  1. colour.md gave Steel the job “graphic mass, the badge skull, rules” — in §2 and again in §5 rule 3. But the badge skull is Bone on Ink: the marks are strictly one colour, and USAGE.md rule 1 forbids Steel for them outright. colour.md was written on 2026-07-31, before the mark existed. Fixed: the phrase is gone from both places, rule 3 now carries the Bone-only consequence gate 5 established, and §2 records the correction.
  2. art-direction.md §10 told Phase 4 that “§2’s ceiling rule is why photographs never out-brighten body text”.
